claim: A Network Load Balancer default action can forward to multiple target groups by relative weight, each from 0 to 999; a weight of 0 sends no traffic, and only new connections follow a weight change.
q: How does a Network Load Balancer split traffic between target groups for a blue/green or canary release?
values: A target group with a weight of 0 receives no traffic
scope: Network Load Balancer listener default action
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-listeners

If you specify multiple target groups for a default action, requests are distributed to these target groups based on their relative weights. You must specify a weight from 0 to 999 for each target group. A target group with a weight of 0 receives no traffic. After you add a target group or update the target group weights, new connections are routed based on the new target group weights. Existing connections are not affected and continue until they are closed as usual.

The Network Load Balancer acts as a pass through load balancer in accordance with [RFC9000](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc9000).
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-listeners
To support both TCP and QUIC on the same port, create a TCP\_QUIC listener.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-listeners

claim: When a zonal shift starts on an Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing enabled, all traffic to targets in the impaired Availability Zone is blocked and the zonal IP addresses are removed from DNS.
q: What happens during a zonal shift on an Application Load Balancer that has cross-zone load balancing on?
values: all traffic to targets is blocked
zonal IP addresses are removed from DNS
scope: Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing enabled
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/zonal-shift

When a zonal shift is started on an Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing enabled, all traffic to targets is blocked in the availability zone being impacted, and zonal IP addresses are removed from DNS.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/zonal-shift
With zonal shift, you can shift traffic away from an impaired Availability Zone with a single action.

claim: Automatic Target Weights (ATW) detects anomalous targets on every Application Load Balancer, but its anomaly mitigation, which routes less traffic to anomalous targets, is only available with the weighted random routing algorithm.
q: Which routing algorithm is needed for an Application Load Balancer to route traffic away from targets with high error rates automatically?
values: reducing the amount of traffic they're routed
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes
The anomaly mitigation function of ATW is only available when using the **Weighted random** routing algorithm.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes
When anomalous targets are identified, ATW can automatically attempt to stabilize them by reducing the amount of traffic they're routed, known as anomaly mitigation.

claim: Application Load Balancer health check logs, which record target health check status and failure reasons, are optional and disabled by default; when enabled they are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket you specify, and you pay only S3 storage.
q: Are Application Load Balancer health check logs on by default, and where do they go?
values: the Amazon S3 bucket that you specify
scope: Application Load Balancer health check logs
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-health-check-logs

Health check logs are an optional feature that is disabled by default. After you enable health check logs for your load balancer, Elastic Load Balancing captures the logs and stores them as compressed files in the Amazon S3 bucket that you specify.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-health-check-logs
You are charged storage costs for Amazon S3, but not charged for the bandwidth used by Elastic Load Balancing to send log files to Amazon S3.

claim: Well-Architected REL10-BP01 says that with cross-zone load balancing enabled, Application and Network Load Balancers detect targets that are unreachable because of an Availability Zone impairment and reroute traffic to targets in healthy Availability Zones.
q: What does Well-Architected say load balancers with cross-zone load balancing do when an Availability Zone is impaired?
values: unreachable due to Availability Zone impairment
reroute traffic towards targets in healthy Availability Zones
scope: AWS Well-Architected Framework, reliability pillar REL10-BP01
ev: docs/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_fault_isolation_multiaz_region_system

If cross-zone load balancing is enabled, [AWS Application Load Balancers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction.html) and [Network Load Balancers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/introduction.html) detect when targets such as EC2 instances and containers are unreachable due to Availability Zone impairment and reroute traffic towards targets in healthy Availability Zones.
